summary: A is closer to the frozen contract and substantially more scope-disciplined. Both candidates incorrectly duplicate Files.Add instead of routing Upload through it, but B additionally changes global request-body replay and Files.Add semantics despite an explicit prohibition on retry refactoring.
reasons: Both Upload implementations correctly use multipartbody.NewFile with field "file", but both bypass FilesService.Add and duplicate its option handling, request, decoding, and missing-data logic.
A limits production changes to the requested convenience API, whereas B adds enableBodyReplay to RawClient.Do, affecting every seekable request body across the SDK.

B changes ownership/closure behavior by replacing a seekable request body such as *os.File with io.NopCloser and reuses the same mutable seeker from GetBody; this is beyond the contract and increases review risk.

B has materially better Upload tests: it verifies filename, content, validation, and an end-to-end 429 replay. A verifies filename but never reads/asserts multipart content, and its retry test only exercises a generic bytes.Reader request rather than Files.Upload itself.
risks_a: Upload does not call FilesService.Add as required, leaving duplicate request and error machinery that can drift.
Tests omit empty-filename and nil-content validation, source-reader failures, multipart content, option propagation, and an end-to-end Upload retry.
The combined validation error is less precise than separate filename and content errors.
risks_b: The global RawClient replay change directly violates the instruction not to refactor unrelated request/retry machinery and changes existing Add/Update behavior.
Upload still bypasses FilesService.Add, violating the required repository reuse pattern.
No test covers propagation of a source-reader failure despite that being explicitly required; option behavior is also not directly verified.
